title: Primality testing: Miller-Rabin (randomized) vs AKS (deterministic)
problem_statement: Given an integer N >= 0, decide whether N is prime.

algorithms.name: Miller-Rabin
algorithms.idea: Write N - 1 = 2^s d with d odd. A base a is a witness of compositeness unless a^d = 1 or a^(2^j d) = -1 mod N for some j < s. For every odd composite N at least 3/4 of the bases 1..N-1 are witnesses.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(k n^3) bit operations for k rounds with schoolbook arithmetic, assuming (machine model, see background) that three-argument pow makes O(n) multiplications mod N, so O(n) per round; Õ(k n^2) if multiplication and division of m-bit integers cost Õ(m)
algorithms.correctness: Primes always pass. With independent uniformly random bases from 2..N-2, an odd composite passes one round with probability < 1/4, so with k >= 1 rounds it is accepted with probability < 4^(-k) (one-sided error). Proved in PROOFS.md, after Rabin 1980.

algorithms.name: AKS
algorithms.idea: Deterministic polynomial-identity test (X + a)^N = X^N + a mod (X^r - 1, N).
algorithms.time_complexity: Õ(n^(21/2)) bit operations if multiplication and division of m-bit integers cost Õ(m), and O(n^(33/2)) with schoolbook arithmetic: polynomial; at least (n - 1)^4 n coefficient operations on every n-bit prime with n >= 24 (proved in ../primality-trial-vs-aks/PROOFS.md, Part A). Faster analyses and variants: see background.
algorithms.correctness: Returns True iff N is prime, for every N >= 0 (proved in ../primality-trial-vs-aks/PROOFS.md, Part A, after Agrawal, Kayal, Saxena 2004).

relationship: Both are polynomial. Miller-Rabin is randomized with one-sided error (it never rejects a prime and accepts a composite with probability < 4^-k for k >= 1 rounds, so PRIMES is in coRP) and takes O(k n^3) bit operations. AKS is deterministic and correct on every input without assumptions, but it performs at least (n - 1)^4 n operations on every n-bit prime with n >= 24: for a fixed number of rounds Miller-Rabin is asymptotically faster on primes, and the proved bounds of AKS have a much larger degree.

sources.title: Primality testing with Gaussian periods
sources.venue: Journal of the European Mathematical Society 21(4), 1229-1269
sources.note: Background only (abstract read): a variant of AKS based on Gaussian periods.

verification.method: Both implementations agree with each other and with a sieve oracle on random n-bit integers, n = 0..20 (AKS up to 16 bits). Miller-Rabin runs 32 rounds with pseudo-random bases (Python's random module, re-seeded by the validator before every call, so the run is reproducible); with independent uniform bases a composite would be accepted with probability < 4^-32. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves the Miller-Rabin claims (the round test, primes always pass, at least 3/4 witnesses, the error bound, time and space, PRIMES in coRP, the comparison with AKS); the AKS claims are proved in ../primality-trial-vs-aks/PROOFS.md. Both name the deterministic tests that check them.

caveats: The V1 run uses pseudo-random bases, so it is a fixed, reproducible computation; the error bound 4^-k is a statement about independent uniform bases. Miller's deterministic variant: see background.
notes: Compare polynomial-identity-testing (staging). The history of the tests: see background.

background.statement: Rabin gives the randomized test; Miller gives a deterministic test that runs in polynomial time assuming the extended Riemann hypothesis; Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena give an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time test.

Lenstra and Pomerance give a deterministic primality test that runs in time (log N)^6 (2 + log log N)^c for an effectively computable constant c; according to their abstract, the same result with 21/2 in place of 6 was proved by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena.

Machine-model assumption, not proved here: Python's three-argument pow(a, d, N) makes O(bitlen(d)) multiplications modulo N (the left-to-right binary method, for example, makes at most 2 bitlen(d)). PROOFS.md, M.5, uses it for the running time.
